abstract: Stripe Economics analysis by Ernie Tedeschi examining whether the recent acceleration in US aggregate productivity can be attributed to AI. The piece accepts the micro-level evidence — Brynjolfsson et al. (2023) on customer service agents 14% more productive, Noy and Zhang (2023) on writers 40% faster, Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) on consultants completing 12% more tasks with 25% less time per task, and Dillon et al. (2025) on knowledge workers saving two hours per week on email across 66 firms — and notes that most of this research used older model generations, so effects may be understated. It then argues that these micro gains are not yet what is driving macro productivity. US labor productivity has grown roughly 2.5% over the past year against a 1.6% two-decade average, and the authors' Markov-switching model puts a 93% probability on the US having entered a high-productivity regime. But total factor productivity, the residual economists treat as pure technological efficiency, has been near zero over the same period under the Fernald estimates maintained by the San Francisco Fed, with under 20% probability of a high-TFP regime. Cross-sectionally, industries with heavy AI adoption in the Census BTOS data do show somewhat stronger recent productivity growth, but those same industries also outperformed in 2016-2019 before generative AI existed; controlling for the pre-existing trend collapses the residual correlation to essentially zero. The proposed reconciliation, drawing on Bank of Korea work (Suh et al. 2026), is that AI compresses time spent on bounded tasks without relaxing the downstream constraints that determine output: adoption cut work time 3.8%, about 1.5 hours per week, but those savings bore essentially no relationship to realized output growth unless workers had the autonomy or incentives to reallocate the freed time.
keyFindings: US labor productivity grew roughly 2.5% over the past year, against a 1.6% annual average across the previous two decades; a Markov-switching model assigns 93% probability that the US has entered a high-productivity regime, though the model says nothing about how long such a regime lasts.

Total factor productivity growth has been near zero over the same period under the Fernald estimates maintained by the San Francisco Fed, with less than 20% probability of a high-TFP-growth regime — the opposite of what frontier-level AI productivity gains should produce.

Combining Census BTOS AI adoption rates with Chicago Fed quarterly industry-level labor productivity yields a positive but modest relationship; however, the same heavy-adopting sectors already showed stronger productivity growth in 2016-2019, and stripping out that pre-existing trend drops the residual correlation to essentially zero.

Bank of Korea research (Suh et al. 2026) finds generative AI adoption reduces work time by 3.8%, about 1.5 hours per week — closely matching the Dillon et al. (2025) two-hours-per-week email finding — but these savings have essentially no relationship with realized output growth unless workers have autonomy or strong incentives to reallocate the saved time.

The micro-level productivity literature is not in dispute: 14% for customer service agents (Brynjolfsson et al. 2023), 40% faster writing (Noy and Zhang 2023), 12% more tasks and 25% less time per task for consultants (Dell'Acqua et al. 2023). The argument is specifically that these gains have not yet aggregated.
methodology: Descriptive macro analysis combining several public sources: BLS labor productivity series; Fernald/San Francisco Fed TFP estimates; Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) AI adoption rates; and Chicago Fed quarterly industry-level labor productivity, which the authors extend two quarters using the Chicago Fed's own methodology. A Markov-switching regime model is used to estimate the probability that labor productivity and TFP have shifted into high-growth states. The industry-level analysis regresses recent productivity growth on self-reported AI adoption, then repeats the exercise controlling for 2016-2019 productivity growth to remove pre-existing sectoral trends.
qualifiers: Tier 2. Published on a Substack (stripeeconomics.com) rather than peer-reviewed, though authored by Ernie Tedeschi, former chief economist at the Council of Economic Advisers, and built on public government data series that can be independently checked. TFP is not directly observable and must be model-estimated, so the near-zero TFP finding inherits the assumptions of the Fernald methodology. The industry-level null is a correlation across a modest number of sectors and cannot rule out that pre-pandemic productivity strength itself caused later AI adoption — the authors state this explicitly. Self-reported BTOS adoption is a coarse measure of actual AI intensity. The piece argues absence of an aggregate effect to date, which is not evidence that no effect will emerge; the authors are careful that a high-productivity regime's duration is unknowable from their model.
